Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

section_titles: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
periods.activity_title: Reading Clocks and Counting Minutes Between Times

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q1–Q3, p.155
tasks_in_class.description: Read the two clock images showing Raghav's yoga start and end times; find how long he spent practising.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c), p.155
tasks_in_class.description: Find the time elapsed between given time periods (01:15 p.m. to 01:42 p.m.; 03:18 p.m. to 08:18 p.m.; 09:15 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.) and share strategies.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q5 (a)(b), p.155
tasks_in_class.description: Using the table of painting times (Raghav 1 hr 20 min, Rani 2 hr 10 min, Ritu 1 hr 35 min), identify who took longest and who took least time.

time_bands.activity: Children examine two clock faces showing Raghav's yoga times. Let us find out Q1–Q3, p.155 ("Read the two clock images showing Raghav's yoga start....") — pairs discuss what they notice about the minute hand positions and how they might find the gap between the two times.

Children work through Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c), p.155 ("Find the time elapsed between given time periods....") in small groups, each group choosing their own counting strategy. Groups then share strategies with the class, the teacher drawing out multiple approaches on the board without prescribing one.

Children read the painting-time table and answer Let us find out Q5 (a)(b), p.155 ("Using the table of painting times, identify who took longest...."). A quick class discussion — 'How did you decide which was longer: 1 hr 20 min or 1 hr 35 min?' — surfaces reasoning about comparing mixed-unit durations.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often read clock faces correctly but subtract the numerals shown rather than counting forward, so 03:18 to 08:18 may yield 5 rather than 5 hours — prompt 'count on from 03:18' to catch this. When comparing mixed-unit times such as 1 hr 20 min and 1 hr 35 min, nudge children to compare the minutes part only once the hours are equal. The 12-hour/24-hour format tasks (Q6 and Q7, p.156) are available as additional practice for fast finishers or for consolidation.
materials: Chalk and board for strategy sharing

section_titles: Reading time and finding elapsed duration

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q6, p.156
tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats in a given table.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us find out Q7, p.156
tasks_in_class.description: Match each time in 12-hour format to its equivalent in 24-hour format.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two or three times on the board in both formats (e.g. 3:00 p.m. and 15:00) and invites children to spot the pattern. A brief class discussion surfaces the rule: afternoon hours gain 12; morning hours before 1:00 p.m. stay the same.

Children complete Let us find out Q6, p.156 ("Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats....") individually. Teacher circulates, noting whether children are adding or subtracting 12 correctly for p.m. and midnight entries.

Children attempt Let us find out Q7, p.156 ("Match each time in 12-hour format to its equivalent in 24-hour format."). Pairs compare answers and reconcile any mismatch, then the class checks together, with the teacher asking 'How did you know this one matched?' to make reasoning explicit.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is adding 12 to a.m. times — children may write 06:00 a.m. as 18:00; remind them only p.m. times (from 1:00 p.m. onwards) gain 12, and midnight is 00:00. The elapsed-time reasoning children did earlier with Raghav's yoga times provides a ready link: knowing whether a time is before or after noon matters for both tasks.

section_titles: Seconds as a unit of time
periods.activity_title: When Minutes Are Not Enough — Discovering Seconds

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate whether each listed activity (blinking, counting 1–20, melting ice-cube, etc.) takes seconds or minutes; tick the appropriate cell.
List events (other than those in the table) that can happen in less than a minute or in a few seconds.
Time yourself: how many times can you skip rope in 10 seconds; how long to write FRIEND; how long to run 100 m.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the walking-race story (Akira, Sunita, Mary all took 1 minute plus seconds) from p.157 aloud. Children discuss: 'Why can't we just say they all took 1 minute?' This surfaces the need for seconds as a finer unit, and '1 minute = 60 seconds' is established together.

Children complete Let Us Do, p.157 ("Estimate whether each listed activity takes seconds or minutes; tick....") individually, then compare with a partner. Class discussion follows: children justify their ticks — 'blinking is quick, so seconds' — building the intuition for sub-minute durations.

Children brainstorm and write their own list for Let Us Do, p.158 ("List events that can happen in less than a minute or in a few seconds."). Pairs share one entry each; the teacher records examples on the board to build a class bank of seconds-scale events.

Children carry out Let Us Find Q1–Q3, p.158 ("Time yourself: skip rope in 10 seconds; write FRIEND; run 100 m.") in a supervised, energetic burst — some tasks in the classroom, the 100 m run noted as a teacher-facilitated outdoor activity or estimated if space is limited. Children record their times.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes confuse 'seconds' with 'very fast' and mark all quick-seeming activities as seconds — draw out that melting an ice cube takes several minutes despite feeling quick to watch. Let Us Do, p.158 (estimate and verify: balloons, push-ups, breaths, hops in one minute) is rich additional practice linking estimation to physical experience; note it for any group that finishes early.
materials: Open space or corridor for 100 m run

section_titles: Reading seconds on a clock face
periods.activity_title: The Third Hand — Reading and Drawing Seconds

tasks_in_class.description: Observe four clock-pair images; read and fill in the number of seconds each child took (getting out of bed, moving to kitchen, picking up paper, washing plate).
Draw the missing seconds hand on the right-side clock for four given durations (20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 40 sec).

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up or draws a large clock face and asks children: 'We know the short hand and the long hand — which hand have we not talked about yet?' Children identify the seconds hand. Together they count the 60 tick marks on a clock face and confirm that one full sweep = 60 seconds = 1 minute.

Children work on Let Us Do, p.159 ("Observe four clock-pair images; read and fill in the number of seconds each child took...."). For each pair of clocks, children count the tick marks the seconds hand has swept. Teacher asks: 'How did you count — by ones, by fives?' to surface efficient counting strategies.

Children attempt Let Us Do, p.160 ("Draw the missing seconds hand on the right-side clock for four given durations...."). They must decide where 20, 30, 60, and 40 seconds land on the face and draw the hand accordingly. Pairs check each other's drawings and discuss any disagreements.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is treating the seconds hand like the minute hand and placing 30 seconds at the 6 but 20 seconds at the 4 (which is correct for minutes but needs checking against tick marks for seconds). The experience of timing physical actions in seconds — from the seconds section — grounds this abstract dial reading in felt duration.
materials: Large demonstration clock face (drawn or printed)

section_titles: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
periods.activity_title: Stretching the Number Line — Hours to Minutes

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the double number line by filling in missing hours and minutes values using the ×2 relationship shown.
Convert: 1 hr 10 min, 2 hr 45 min, 3 hr 15 min, 4 hr 20 min to minutes; and 75 min, 150 min, 220 min, 390 min to hours and minutes.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a double number line on the board: top track in hours (1, 2, 3, …), bottom track in minutes (60, 120, 180, …). Children fill in gaps and explain what 'doubles' means here. The pattern '× 60 each time' is made explicit by the class together, echoing the characters' dialogue in the book (p.161).

Children complete Let Us Do Q1(a), p.161 ("Complete the double number line by filling in missing hours and minutes values....") in their books. Teacher checks that children are using multiplication (×60) rather than repeated addition only, and nudges those who are adding 60 repeatedly to see the shortcut.

Children work through Let Us Do Q1(b)(i–viii), p.161 ("Convert 1 hr 10 min, 2 hr 45 min … to minutes; and 75 min, 150 min … to hours and minutes."). Teacher circulates; pairs who finish discuss how they handled remainders (e.g. 75 ÷ 60 = 1 hr 15 min). A few examples are shared with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Children converting mixed quantities such as 2 hr 45 min often multiply only the whole hours (120 min) and forget to add the remaining 45 min — prompt 'What about the extra minutes?' The double number line scaffold makes the multiplicative structure visible; encourage children to refer back to it when they are unsure rather than guessing.
materials: Chalk and board for number line
Squared paper for individual number lines

section_titles: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
periods.activity_title: Scaling to Seconds — Minutes on the Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Fill the min↔sec double number line; convert 320 sec, 225 sec, 700 sec, 1000 sec to min and sec; convert 10 min 13 sec, 4 min 8 sec, 15 min 40 sec to seconds.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a quick oral warm-up: 'We know 1 minute = 60 seconds. How many seconds in 2 minutes? 3 minutes?' Children call out answers, connecting the new number line to the hours-to-minutes pattern from their earlier conversion work. The min↔sec double number line is drawn on the board.

Children fill in the min↔sec double number line and begin the first half of Let Us Do Q1(c)(i–vii), p.162 ("Fill the min↔sec double number line; convert 320 sec, 225 sec … to min and sec...."). Teacher prompts: 'Divide by 60 — what is the quotient and what is the remainder?' to make the division structure explicit.

Children complete the remaining conversions in Let Us Do Q1(c)(i–vii), p.162 (converting 10 min 13 sec, 4 min 8 sec, 15 min 40 sec to seconds). Groups compare answers for the larger values (700 sec, 1000 sec) and discuss where the remainder goes. A pair presents one tricky conversion to the class with their reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Children converting 1000 seconds often make an error of treating 1000 ÷ 60 as 16 remainder 0 rather than 16 remainder 40 — encourage them to verify by multiplying back (16 × 60 = 960; 1000 − 960 = 40). The connection to the racing context — all three runners' times in seconds — helps children see why the conversion matters beyond a drill.
materials: Chalk and board for number line

section_titles: Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
periods.activity_title: Counting On to Solve Time Stories

tasks_in_class.description: Raghav studies 4 subjects at 50 minutes each; find total time in hours and minutes and share strategies.
Raghu leaves at 08:00 hours and arrives at 09:05 hours; find time taken to reach Nana ji's house.

Solve word problems: find return/finish time given start time and duration, or find start time given finish time and duration (Jyoti, Ragini, picnic group, Raji, Alya, lunch break, 08:35 PM problems).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the worked example from the book: Raghu travels from 08:00 to 09:05 hours — how long? Children try to solve it mentally before the teacher walks through the oral strategy: count 1 whole hour to 09:00, then 5 more minutes. Children articulate why this avoids subtraction errors across the hour boundary.

Children solve Let Us Do Q2, p.162 ("Raghav studies 4 subjects at 50 minutes each; find total time....") and Q3, p.162 ("Raghu leaves at 08:00 hours and arrives at 09:05 hours; find time taken...."). Pairs share oral strategies — no column algorithms; the teacher records different methods side by side on the board.

Children work through Let Us Do Q4–Q10, p.163 ("Solve word problems: find return/finish time given start time and duration, or find start time...."). Teacher circulates, prompting children who are stuck: 'Start at the known time and count forward.' A few problems are reviewed together, with children explaining their reasoning aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often add durations to the wrong part of a mixed time — for instance, adding 1 hour 30 minutes to 08:45 by writing 09:75, forgetting to regroup the 75 minutes. Encourage the count-on strategy: jump to the next whole hour first, then add remaining minutes. The conversion knowledge from hours and minutes to minutes — built in the double number line work — supports checking answers here.
materials: Chalk and board for strategy display

section_titles: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
Seconds as a unit of time
Reading seconds on a clock face
Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
periods.activity_title: Racing Seconds — A Whole-Chapter Time Challenge

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the three units of time as a class: seconds, minutes, hours. Children call out the key relationships (1 min = 60 sec, 1 hr = 60 min) and say one real-life event for each unit. Teacher then introduces a 'time relay' challenge: a set of five mixed questions, one from each part of the chapter, to be answered as a class team.

Groups of four receive five questions covering: reading a clock face including the seconds hand; estimating whether an activity takes seconds or minutes; converting a mixed time (e.g. 2 hr 30 min to minutes, 125 sec to min and sec); reading 24-hour format; and finding elapsed time between two given times. Groups discuss and record answers.

Each group presents one answer to the class, explaining their method. Teacher draws connections across the chapter: 'You used the 60-seconds rule you discovered with the walking race when you converted 125 seconds; you used the count-on strategy from the word-problem section when you found elapsed time.' Children hear the chapter's ideas named and linked.

Children individually write one time fact they found surprising and one situation in their own day where they now think in seconds, minutes, or hours. A quick round-the-class share closes the unit on a reflective, personal note.

periods.teacher_notes: The five relay questions should draw on all five sections of the chapter — reading time, seconds as a unit, the seconds hand, conversion, and word problems — so every concept is revisited. If a group struggles with the conversion question, prompt them to sketch a double number line from memory; this checks whether the scaffold has become a mental tool.
materials: Printed or board-written relay question set
Pencils and paper for individual reflection

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Write two things you can do in less than a minute and two things that take more than a minute. For each one, say how you know which group it belongs to.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Answers will vary. Acceptable examples of under-a-minute events include blinking, clapping ten times, writing your name. Over-a-minute examples include boiling water, eating a meal. Children should give a reason based on how quickly or slowly the action finishes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the action's felt duration against the 60-second span of one minute.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child act out each event and count aloud; stretch: ask them to order all four items from quickest to slowest.

exercise.description: List events (other than those in the table) that can happen in less than a minute or in a few seconds.

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Priya says she can write the word MATHEMATICS in about 15 seconds. Do you think this is too fast, about right, or too slow? Write one sentence explaining your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: MATHEMATICS has 11 letters. Writing one letter takes roughly 1–2 seconds, so 11 letters would take roughly 11–22 seconds. 15 seconds is a reasonable estimate — about right. Children who timed themselves writing FRIEND (6 letters) can scale up.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate by counting letters and using personal timing experience to scale the duration.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write FRIEND while counting seconds aloud, then compare; stretch: ask how long it would take to write their full name and explain the reasoning.

exercise.description: Time yourself: how many times can you skip rope in 10 seconds; how long to write FRIEND; how long to run 100 m.

items.section_title: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
items.prompt: Meena starts reading at 10:40 a.m. and stops at 11:15 a.m. How long did she read?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 35 minutes. Count from 10:40 to 11:00 = 20 minutes, then 11:00 to 11:15 = 15 minutes; total = 35 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward to the next whole hour, then add the remaining minutes.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child subtracted 40 − 15 = 25, ignoring the hour change.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child subtracted 40 from 11:25 or added an extra 10 minutes erroneously.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child misread 11:15 as 1 hour 15 minutes past 10:00 without accounting for the 40-minute start.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 10:40 to 11:15 and count the jumps; stretch: ask what time she would finish if she read for another 25 minutes.

exercise.book_ref: Let us find out Q4 (a)(b)(c), p.155
exercise.description: Find the time elapsed between given time periods (01:15 p.m. to 01:42 p.m.; 03:18 p.m. to 08:18 p.m.; 09:15 a.m. to 11:30 a.m.) and share strategies.

items.section_title: Seconds as a unit of time
items.prompt: Three friends complete a short race. Anu finishes in 1 minute 8 seconds, Bina in 1 minute 14 seconds, and Charu in 58 seconds. Who wins the race?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Charu wins. Her time of 58 seconds is less than 1 minute, while Anu took 68 seconds and Bina took 74 seconds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert all times to seconds (1 min = 60 sec) and compare: 68, 74, and 58 seconds.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child may have compared only the seconds digits (8 < 14) without considering Charu's time.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child may have chosen the name that appeared last or misread the times.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child incorrectly grouped two runners or misunderstood 'wins'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write all three times in seconds on a number line and compare; stretch: ask by how many seconds Charu beat Anu.

exercise.description: Estimate whether each listed activity (blinking, counting 1–20, melting ice-cube, etc.) takes seconds or minutes; tick the appropriate cell.

items.section_title: Reading seconds on a clock face
items.prompt: A seconds hand points to 12 at the start. After Raju washes his hands, the seconds hand points to 9. How many seconds did Raju take? Explain how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 45 seconds. The seconds hand moves from 12 to 9, which is three-quarters of the clock face. Three-quarters of 60 seconds = 45 seconds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the tick marks swept from 12 to 9 on the clock face (each mark = 1 second; 9 × 5 = 45).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child count individual tick marks on a printed clock face; stretch: ask where the hand would point if Raju took 50 seconds instead.

exercise.description: Observe four clock-pair images; read and fill in the number of seconds each child took (getting out of bed, moving to kitchen, picking up paper, washing plate).

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: A double number line shows: 1 hour = 60 minutes, 2 hours = 120 minutes. Deepa says 3 hours = 170 minutes. Is she right? Write one sentence to explain your answer.
items.visual_stimulus:
number_line: 1 hr | 2 hr | 3 hr | 4 hr
number_line: 60 min | 120 min | ... | ...

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Deepa is wrong. 3 hours = 3 × 60 = 180 minutes, not 170 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of hours by 60 to find the total minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to extend the number line one step at a time (60, 120, 180); stretch: ask what 4 hours and 30 minutes equals in minutes.

exercise.description: Complete the double number line by filling in missing hours and minutes values using the ×2 relationship shown.

items.section_title: Reading time and finding elapsed duration
items.prompt: Which of these shows 3:30 p.m. in 24-hour format?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15:30. For p.m. times from 1:00 p.m. onwards, add 12 to the hours: 3 + 12 = 15.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 12 to the hour for any p.m. time from 1:00 p.m. to 11:59 p.m.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child wrote the 12-hour digits unchanged, treating p.m. like a.m.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child added 10 instead of 12, or confused the rule.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child converted the hour correctly but dropped the minutes.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out the rule (hour + 12 for p.m.) and apply it step by step; stretch: convert 11:45 p.m. and 12:10 a.m. to 24-hour format and explain the special cases.

exercise.book_ref: Let us find out Q6, p.156
exercise.description: Fill in the blanks converting between 12-hour and 24-hour time formats in a given table.

items.section_title: Reading seconds on a clock face
items.prompt: Draw a clock face and mark where the seconds hand should point to show exactly 30 seconds. Then write the number of tick marks the hand has swept from the 12.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The seconds hand points to the 6 (directly at the bottom of the clock). It has swept 30 tick marks from the 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: 30 seconds is half of 60 seconds, so the hand is halfway around the clock face, pointing to the 6.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a printed clock outline with tick marks already drawn; stretch: ask the child to also draw where the hand would point at 15 seconds and at 45 seconds.

exercise.description: Draw the missing seconds hand on the right-side clock for four given durations (20 sec, 30 sec, 60 sec, 40 sec).

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: A film lasts 2 hours and 15 minutes. How many minutes is that in total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the hours by 60 to get minutes, then add the remaining minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a double number line up to 2 hours and add 15 minutes at the end; stretch: ask how many seconds the film lasts in total.

exercise.description: Convert: 1 hr 10 min, 2 hr 45 min, 3 hr 15 min, 4 hr 20 min to minutes; and 75 min, 150 min, 220 min, 390 min to hours and minutes.

items.section_title: Converting between hours, minutes, and seconds
items.prompt: A runner completes a lap in 245 seconds. Express this time in minutes and seconds.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 minutes 5 seconds. 245 ÷ 60 = 4 remainder 5, so 4 minutes and 5 seconds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total seconds by 60; the quotient is minutes and the remainder is seconds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use the double number line (1 min = 60 sec) and count up in sixties: 60, 120, 180, 240, then 5 more; stretch: ask how many more seconds the runner would need to make the time exactly 5 minutes.

exercise.description: Fill the min↔sec double number line; convert 320 sec, 225 sec, 700 sec, 1000 sec to min and sec; convert 10 min 13 sec, 4 min 8 sec, 15 min 40 sec to seconds.

items.section_title: Time word problems — elapsed, start, and end time
items.prompt: Arjun's cricket practice starts at 04:30 p.m. and lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. At what time does his practice end?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 06:15 p.m. Count forward 1 hour from 04:30 to 05:30, then add 45 minutes: 05:30 + 45 minutes = 06:15 p.m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward by whole hours first, then add the remaining minutes.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 04:30 on a number line and draw two jumps — one of 1 hour, one of 45 minutes; stretch: ask what time Arjun must leave home if he needs 20 minutes to travel to the ground.

exercise.description: Solve word problems: find return/finish time given start time and duration, or find start time given finish time and duration (Jyoti, Ragini, picnic group, Raji, Alya, lunch break, 08:35 PM problems).
